title: The Middle Ages · Episode 1
chapters: The real life of a medieval knight

units.t: The Middle Ages. Episode one.
In this episode: Castles, kings and feudalism, The real life of a medieval knight, Myths about the Middle Ages and The Vikings.
Part one. Castles, kings and feudalism.
Lords, knights, peasants and castles.
How medieval Europe organised power when there was no strong central state.
The Middle Ages, rethought.
The Middle Ages stretch from the collapse of the western Roman Empire in the 400s to around 1500, the age of the printing press, the voyages to the Americas and the Reformation.
Later writers saw a gap between two brilliant eras and called it the 'Dark Ages'.
Historians now avoid that label: the period gave us great cathedrals, universities, new farming technology and lively trade, alongside war and plague.
Many popular ideas are myths.
Educated medieval people knew the Earth was round; the flat-Earth story spread in the 1800s.
Low life expectancy mostly reflects child deaths, and adults often reached their fifties or sixties.
Always ask which century and which place, because a thousand years across a continent was never one world.
Land for loyalty.
With no strong central state, power rested on land.
A king granted estates, called fiefs, to powerful nobles.
In return they knelt to do homage, swore an oath of fealty and supplied knights for his wars, often for around 40 days a year.
Those nobles granted land to lesser lords and knights on similar terms.
Historians debate how neat this 'feudal pyramid' really was, and practice varied by place and century.
Knights trained from boyhood, first as pages, then as squires.
Armour, a warhorse and weapons were hugely expensive, which is why knights needed land.
Chivalry, a code praising courage, loyalty and protecting the weak, grew in the 1100s and filled tales like King Arthur's.
Real knights often fell short of it, especially towards peasants.
Peasants and plague.
About nine in ten people worked the land.
Many were serfs: not enslaved, but not free.
They couldn't leave the manor without permission, owed labour on the lord's fields and paid dues, in return for protection and strips of land to farm.
They ate mostly bread, pottage and ale, and a failed harvest could bring famine.
Then came the Black Death.
Plague reached Europe on trading ships in 1347 and killed perhaps a third to half of the population within four years.
With workers scarce, survivors could demand higher wages or move.
Lords tried to freeze wages, as England's Statute of Labourers did in 1351, and the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 followed.
It failed, but serfdom largely faded in England and western Europe, though it strengthened in parts of eastern Europe.
Castles and cannons.
Early castles, from the 900s and 1000s, were often wooden towers on earth mounds, called motte-and-bailey castles.
After 1066 the Normans built hundreds across England to hold down the conquered population.
Stone castles followed, with thick walls, towers, moats and gatehouses, like the Tower of London's White Tower.
A castle was a home, a military base, a prison, a courthouse and a symbol of power.
Attackers used siege towers, trebuchets, catapult-like machines, tunnels and starvation.
Gunpowder cannons, increasingly powerful through the 1400s, made tall stone walls vulnerable, and the age of castles faded.
The Church.
The Church shaped daily life from baptism to burial.
It owned huge amounts of land, collected tithes, a tenth of income, ran its own courts and offered one of the few paths to education.
Monasteries copied books by hand, preserving ancient texts, and ran hospitals and schools.
The first universities, such as Bologna, Paris and Oxford, grew up with strong church links.
Popes and kings often competed for power.
Great Gothic cathedrals, like Notre-Dame in Paris and Chartres, with their soaring vaults and stained glass, took generations to build.
The key idea: The Middle Ages ran from Rome's fall in the 400s to about 1500, and the 'Dark Ages' label is misleading.
Part two. The real life of a medieval knight.
Forget cranes lifting clanking men onto horses.
Real knights were trained athletes, expensive to equip, and often far less chivalrous than the stories suggest.
Page, squire, knight.
Becoming a knight was not a matter of simply buying a sword.
In the classic pattern, a boy from a noble family was sent at around seven to serve in another lord’s household as a page.
He learnt manners, riding, basic weapon handling and how to serve at table.
At around fourteen he became a squire, attached to a knight whose armour he cleaned, whose horses he tended and whom he followed onto the battlefield.
If he proved himself, he might be dubbed a knight around twenty-one, sometimes in a solemn ceremony and sometimes in a hurry on the eve of battle.
Ages varied a great deal, but the idea was constant: knighthood was earned through years of service.
An expensive business.
A knight was in many ways a very expensive piece of military equipment.
He needed armour, a sword, a lance, a shield, squires and servants, and above all horses.
The finest warhorses, called destriers, were specially bred and trained for the noise and violence of battle, and could cost many times the price of an ordinary horse.
He also needed riding horses for travel and pack horses for baggage.
This is why knights were usually supported by land.
In return for military service, a lord granted them estates whose peasants produced the income.
The cost was so heavy that, by the 1200s, the English crown was ordering qualified landowners to become knights, and many paid fines to avoid it.
Armour and heraldry.
Films show knights hoisted onto horses by cranes, helpless if they fell.
That is a myth, popularised in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
A complete suit of plate armour, at its peak in the 1400s, typically weighed twenty to twenty-five kilograms, less than many modern soldiers carry.
Because the weight was spread across the body, a fit man could run, mount a horse and get up after a fall.
The real cost was stamina: experiments with volunteers in replica armour found walking and running took roughly twice the energy.
Full-face helmets from the twelfth century made knights hard to identify, so they painted bold designs on shields and on the cloth surcoats worn over armour, hence ‘coat of arms’.
These became hereditary, tracked by heralds.
Many modern logos still borrow the look.
Tournaments and fame.
Tournaments started in the eleventh and twelfth centuries as something close to real war.
Teams of knights charged each other across open countryside in a mêlée, capturing opponents and holding them for ransom.
People were injured and killed, and the Church repeatedly condemned them.
For a skilled but landless knight, though, they were a path to fortune.
William Marshal, an English knight of the late twelfth century, reportedly captured hundreds of opponents and rose to become one of the most powerful men in England.
Later tournaments became more organised and theatrical, with jousting, in which two knights charged each other with lances, often separated by a barrier.
Champions became celebrities, and spectators watched from decorated stands.
Chivalry: ideal and reality.
Chivalry described an ideal knight: brave, loyal to his lord, generous, courteous and devoted to the Church.
Poets and romances about King Arthur and his knights spread these values, and many knights took them seriously.
Rules of conduct also had practical benefits, since a captured noble was usually worth more alive, for ransom, than dead.
But chivalry mostly applied between knights.
Ordinary soldiers and peasants often received no such mercy.
Medieval armies regularly practised the chevauchée, a raid that deliberately burned villages and crops to ruin an enemy’s economy.
The gap between the ideal and reality was obvious even at the time, and many medieval writers criticised knights for their cruelty and greed.
The key idea: Knighthood was earned through years of service, usually starting as a page at around seven.
Part three. Myths about the Middle Ages.
Flat Earth, no baths, and everyone dead by thirty.
Much of what people think they know about medieval life was invented or exaggerated centuries later.
Myth: a flat Earth.
One of the most persistent ideas about the Middle Ages is that people believed the Earth was flat, and that Columbus had to prove otherwise.
In fact, educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was a sphere.
Ancient Greek scholars had shown this, and writers such as the English monk Bede in the eighth century took it for granted.
A thirteenth-century astronomy textbook, De sphaera, taught a spherical Earth in universities for centuries.
Kings were even shown holding an orb, a globe symbolising their rule.
The argument over Columbus’s voyage was about the size of the Earth, and his critics were right that it was larger than he claimed.
The flat Earth myth spread mostly in the 1800s.
Myth: dead by thirty.
You may have heard that medieval people lived to around thirty.
Estimates of average life expectancy at birth in that range are plausible, but averages can mislead.
A huge share of children died in infancy or early childhood from disease, and these deaths pulled the average down sharply.
If a family had one child who died as a baby and another who lived to sixty, their average is about thirty, yet no one died at thirty.
People who survived childhood had a reasonable chance of reaching their fifties or sixties, and some lived much longer.
Old people were a normal part of medieval communities.
Dangers for adults were real, including childbirth, plague, war and accidents, but thirty was not old age.
Myths: baths and water.
Medieval people did not have modern plumbing, but they were not indifferent to dirt.
Washing hands before and after meals was expected etiquette, people washed their faces and bodies with water from basins, and soap was made and sold across Europe.
Many towns had public bathhouses, often called stews in England.
These became associated with prostitution, and many closed in the sixteenth century, partly because of fears that they spread disease, including syphilis.
The claim that people drank beer because all water was deadly is also exaggerated.
They preferred clean springs, wells and rivers, and towns built fountains and pipes.
Medical writings sometimes recommended water.
Ale was popular because it was cheap, calorie-rich and enjoyable, and much everyday ale was fairly weak.
Myths: belts and witches.
The image of a crusading knight locking his wife into an iron chastity belt is a favourite of comedies and tourist museums.
Historians find almost no reliable evidence for it.
The earliest mentions are a handful of fifteenth-century references, several seemingly jokes about jealous husbands.
Many belts once displayed in museums are eighteenth- or nineteenth-century creations.
Wearing one for long would cause serious infections.
Witch hunts are also often placed in the Middle Ages.
In fact, the large-scale hunts mostly came in the early modern period, peaking roughly between 1560 and 1630.
Earlier, an early medieval Church text, the Canon Episcopi, treated witches flying at night as an illusion.
Belief in organised, devil-worshipping witches grew in the fifteenth century, helped by the Malleus Maleficarum of 1486 and the printing press.
Estimates suggest forty to sixty thousand executions, not millions.
Myth: the Dark Ages.
In the fourteenth century, the Italian scholar Petrarch helped popularise the idea that the centuries after Rome’s fall were a time of darkness compared with classical antiquity.
The label stuck, but most historians now avoid it.
The early medieval period does have fewer written sources in some regions, which makes it darker to us in the sense of being harder to see.
But the medieval centuries also produced the first European universities, such as Bologna, Paris and Oxford, soaring Gothic cathedrals, mechanical clocks, eyeglasses and the spread of windmills.
Monasteries copied and preserved many classical texts.
Meanwhile, scholars in the Islamic world, Byzantium and China were making major advances.
The Middle Ages were not a pause in history.
The key idea: Educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was a sphere; the flat Earth story mostly arose in the 1800s.
Part four. The Vikings.
Raiders, yes, but also traders, farmers, explorers and settlers who reached from Baghdad to North America.
Who were the Vikings.
The Vikings came from what's now Norway, Sweden and Denmark.
Strictly, 'going viking' meant going on an overseas raid; most Scandinavians were farmers, fishers and craftspeople who stayed home.
The Viking Age is often dated from the raid on Lindisfarne monastery in 793 to the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066, where the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada died invading England.
And no, they didn't wear horned helmets: that image comes from 1800s costume designs, especially for Wagner's operas.
Society was layered.
Jarls were chieftains, karls were free farmers who could speak at local assemblies called things, and thralls were enslaved people, often captured in raids.
Women ran the household and could own property and seek divorce.
Longships and trade.
Built of overlapping planks, the longship was flexible, fast under sail or oars, and so shallow it could travel far up rivers.
Raiders could strike deep inland and leave before defenders gathered; in 845 a fleet sailed up the Seine and attacked Paris.
Broader cargo ships, called knarrs, carried trade and settlers.
Monasteries were wealthy, poorly defended targets, and Vikings demanded payments to leave, which the English called Danegeld.
But trade mattered as much.
Swedish Vikings, known as the Rus, travelled Russian rivers to Constantinople and Baghdad, trading furs, amber and enslaved people for silver and silk.
Some served in the Byzantine emperor's Varangian Guard.
Viking settlers.
Vikings didn't only raid; they settled.
Much of northern and eastern England became the Danelaw.
Place names ending in -by or -thorpe, like Whitby and Grimsby, are Norse, and York, their Jorvik, became a major Viking town.
They founded Dublin.
In France, Vikings settled the region that became Normandy, 'land of the Northmen'.
Their Norman descendants conquered England in 1066.
Norse settlers colonised Iceland from around 870, where in 930 they created one of the world's oldest parliaments, the Althing.
Reaching America.
From Iceland, Erik the Red founded settlements in Greenland in the 980s.
His son Leif Erikson sailed further west around the year 1000, reaching a land the Norse called Vinland.
For centuries this was known only from Icelandic sagas.
Then, in the 1960s, archaeologists found a Norse site at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, and tree-ring evidence dates wood cut there to 1021.
The Norse didn't stay: distance, small numbers and conflict with local peoples made a lasting colony impossible.
The sagas themselves were mostly written in Iceland in the 1200s and 1300s, so historians treat them as a mix of memory and storytelling, and rely on archaeology, runestones and DNA to check them.
Gods and legacy.
Vikings worshipped gods including Odin, the wise one-eyed chief god; Thor, the thunder god with his hammer; and Freyja, goddess of love and war.
Warriors who died bravely hoped to reach Valhalla, Odin's great hall.
By around 1100, much of Scandinavia had converted to Christianity, often led by kings.
Their legacy lingers.
Wednesday is Woden's, Odin's, day and Thursday is Thor's day.
English borrowed hundreds of Norse words, including sky, egg, knife, window and even 'they'.
Bluetooth takes its name from the Danish king Harald Bluetooth.
The key idea: Vikings were seafaring Scandinavians from about AD 793 to 1066, and most Scandinavians never went raiding.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do historians now avoid calling the period the 'Dark Ages'?
Answer. It had real achievements, such as universities.
Question two. How did a boy typically become a knight in the classic pattern?
Answer. Years of service as a page, then a squire.
Question three. What was the real argument about Columbus’s voyage?
Answer. The size of the Earth, not its shape.
Question four. Where does the image of Vikings in horned helmets come from?
Answer. Opera costume designs in the 1800s.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
